props.title: Data, Secrets & Caching
props.sub: how information flows through a run

notes.t: GITHUB_ENV — a variable for every later step
GITHUB_PATH — add a folder to PATH
::add-mask:: — hide a value created at runtime
::warning:: / ::error:: — annotations on the run and the PR
GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY — a markdown report on the run page

captions: Part six. Data.

Workflows need to make decisions, keep secrets, pass
results
along, and remember things between runs.

Anything inside dollar, double braces is an
expression, evaluated
by GitHub.

Expressions read from contexts. github holds the
event, the

branch and the actor. env holds variables. secrets
holds

secrets. And matrix, needs, steps and inputs hold
what
you'd expect.
The most common use is if, on a job
or a step.
This deploy step runs only on a push to
main, and only if everything before it succeeded.
Watch it evaluate for four different runs. Only one
passes.

There are status functions too: success, failure,
always and
cancelled. always is handy for cleanup that must run
no matter what.
Configuration comes in three kinds.

env sets plain environment variables, right in the
workflow
file.

Variables, the vars context, live in settings —
non-secret
config like a region or a URL.

Secrets are encrypted. They're stored at the
organization, repository
or environment level, and the narrowest scope wins.
Secrets never appear in plain text. If one is
printed, the log shows three stars instead.
But masking isn't magic. If you transform a secret
— encode it, or split it — the log
won't recognise it. So don't print secrets at all.
Steps and jobs often need to pass results along.
Inside a job, a step writes a key and
a value to a special file, named GitHub output.
Later steps read it through the steps context.
Between jobs it's different — they run on different
machines. A job declares outputs, and the next job
reads them through needs.
For files, like a compiled app or a test

report, use artifacts. Upload in one job, download
in
another.
Artifacts also appear on the run page for people
to download, kept for ninety days by default.
Remember, every job starts on a clean machine. So

without help, every run downloads all its
dependencies again.
Caching fixes that. You save a folder under a
key, and restore it next time.
The trick is the key. It includes a hash
of your lock file. Same lock file, same key
— a cache hit, and installing takes seconds.

Change one dependency, and the hash changes. New
key,
a miss, a fresh install — and a new
cache saved for next time.
Most setup actions do this for you with one
cache option. Each repo gets ten gigabytes of cache

free, and unused entries are evicted after seven
days.
Steps can also talk back to the runner.

Besides GitHub output, there are more special files.
Write
to GitHub env, and a variable exists for every
later step. Write to GitHub path, and a folder
joins the path.
Then there are workflow commands — special lines you

echo. add-mask hides a value you generated at
runtime,
like a temporary token.

warning and error create annotations, shown on the
run
page and even on the pull request diff.
And the step summary file turns markdown into a
report on the run page — tables, results and
links.
